item.title: The Ripple Effect of Going for It
item.description: Can you learn to captain a yacht at 62 and turn it into a world-traveling lifestyle? Absolutely! Below, Sine Maria shares a first-hand account of her family’s latest charter with Dream Yacht in the Balearic Islands. Read on for an inspiring look at courage, partnership, and what happens when you say yes to a new adventure on the water. The Ripple Effect of Going for It On breaking into worlds you weren’t born into, and what happens when you actually do the thing. By: Good Life Designed and Sine Maria If there’s one thing I’ve learned from my mom, it’s that life has so much to offer and the limit of your world is only limited by your ability to keep expanding. In the middle of the pandemic, as part of our collective pause, she and I decided to go through the whole Good Life Designed program together again. It was through that process that she decided she wanted to be closer to nature, swim more, and learn how to sail. She didn’t grow up around sailing, knew it was costly and a bit of a boys club, but always admired the access it gave those who knew how. That hobby could take you anywhere in the world. The world of sailing requires a unique blend of resources, courage, technical education, practice, and willing crew members to go along for the ride and be there while you figure things out on your first trips alone. It thrives behind heavy yacht club doors that some are born with access into – but most don’t even know exist. The dream of being certified as a sailor has an even smaller niche- attracting those who thrive on the pressure to read and respond to the chaos of the elements at sea while holding the responsibility of passengers’ lives in their hands. Now that I have experienced the reward that comes with that kind of responsibility – I see the draw. Breaking Into a World You Weren’t Born Into I tried to look into data about women certified sailors but couldn’t find any credible data because no one seems to be particularly interested in that stat – however I can tell you there aren’t many. Sailing, just due to the nature of it, the time it requires, the unease that comes with the experience, especially as you’re getting your first solo trips under your belt, is enough to send anyone right over the edge. It’s heady, it’s overwhelming, it’s complicated, it’s technical, and it feels uncertain and dangerous before you’re skilled and experienced enough to feel truly comfortable and at ease on the water. When Pernille got the ping to learn to sail, the biggest question was how, as a 62-year-old woman, was she going to do it. She tried visiting yacht clubs but as someone who wasn’t interested in the social component and was really looking for the technical skills to captain her own ship, it didn’t feel like the best place to spend her time or money. The classes and day sail opportunities to get out on the water were nice, but if she really wanted to learn everything she needed to, she needed something different. She came across Nautilus Sailing, a week-long course in the Sea of Cortez that would teach you everything you need to know about sailing and cap off the week with a test that would certify you to sail on your own anywhere in the world. My dad at the time was in the most stressful period of his career, navigating his independent school and their 400 families through Covid. Using his coveted spring break to learn to navigate another set of uncharted territories felt not quite like the vacation he needed. But he took a leap of his own and joined her anyway. They spent a week disconnected from everything to focus on learning the thing that would later give them access to the life they live now – barely imaginable to them then. Heading out on what feel like once-in-a-lifetime week long sailing experiences all over the world with friends and family. item.title: French Polynesia Cabin Cruise: The Floating Boutique Hotel for Effortless Island Hopping
item.description: Imagine waking up in a comfortable suite aboard a premium catamaran. You stretch out on crisp sheets and wonder what spectacular view is awaiting you today. Will it be the majestic twin peaks of Bora Bora or the white sand beaches and tropical jungles of Huahine? You step on deck and sniff the air: today’s port is actually the vanilla-scented shores of Taha’a. That’s what life is like aboard a French Polynesia cabin cruise. Every day, you get to go on a new adventure. At night, you rest and relax in the comfort of a spacious cabin aboard a shared catamaran charter. For many travelers, the freedom to visit multiple destinations rather than be confined to a single resort makes a cabin cruise a much better option than a typical holiday on land. What Is a French Polynesia Cabin Cruise? A French Polynesia catamaran cruise or cabin cruise is a travel option where you book a private cabin with its own attached bathroom on a catamaran. Instead of chartering an entire yacht yourself, you share the vessel with a small group of other travelers. How Cabin Cruises Work The catamaran operates much like a small-scale cruise ship but with a personalized touch. Your captain navigates the islands, and an onboard steward prepares your meals. This vacation style eliminates the stress of trip planning, sailing logistics, and meal preparation. And since vessels are shared among travelers, cabin cruises are more affordable than booking Tahiti yacht charters . Why It Feels Like a Floating Boutique Hotel Unlike massive cruise ships that carry thousands of passengers, a catamaran hosts between 8 and 12 guests. This creates an intimate atmosphere, similar to that of a small hotel, except you also get to experience different destinations and activities every day. In French Polynesia, our cabin cruises are offered on the Bali 5.4, Lagoon 620, and the Fountaine Pajot Ipanema 58, each accommodating 12 guests. Comfort and Convenience: What Is a Cabin Cruise Like Onboard? Life aboard a cabin charter is defined by relaxation and comfort. Your catamaran features decks, shaded outdoor dining areas, and a forward trampoline net. This net is a great spot to lounge as the islands glide by. No jostling for sunbathing space on crowded beaches or lining up to rent gear from stands along the shore. You can get all the sun you want on deck, and the cruise includes the use of water sports equipment. You can step directly off the yacht’s transom steps into the water, swim, snorkel, or kayak to your heart’s content. Island Hopping Without Repacking or Airport Transfers With 118 islands and atolls spread across an area as vast as Western Europe, French Polynesia island hopping is all about discovering the unique character of each destination. However, having your base camp be a hotel or resort limits your options. It also means you have to go through a drawn-out process of getting there before you can visit each different island. Traditional travelers must pack their suitcases, check out of their resorts, take a taxi to the airport, wait in security lines, and fly to the next island, only to repeat the check-in process. Meanwhile, on Tahiti cabin cruises , you unpack your bags once on arrival. While you relax on deck or sleep in your cabin, the catamaran moves you between Tahiti and other destinations like Huahine, Raiatea, Taha’a, and Bora Bora. A Tahiti cabin charter eliminates the need for regional flights and ferry schedules, saving you both travel stress and vacation time. Space, Food, Privacy, and Seasickness: Honest Answers Before booking a sailing trip, it is normal to have a few questions about how things work on a boat. Here is what daily life aboard your shared luxury catamaran looks like. Space: Yacht cabins are smaller than hotel rooms, but they’re just as well-appointed. item.title: Top Things to See and Do on a Yacht Charter in Thailand
item.description: Thailand is a spectacular destination for yacht charters, offering a blend of natural beauty, vibrant culture, and unforgettable sailing experiences. A yacht charter from our base in Phuket offers access to some of Thailand’s most stunning and exotic destinations. With its beautiful beaches, crystal-clear waters, and spectacular marine life, Phuket is the perfect starting point for an unforgettable sailing adventure. Here are the top things to see and do on a yacht charter in Thailand. 1. Explore Phang Nga Bay One of the most iconic sailing destinations from Phuket, Phang Nga Bay is renowned for its towering limestone karsts rising dramatically from the emerald-green waters. The bay offers excellent sailing conditions and numerous islands to explore. Among the highlights is James Bond Island (Koh Tapu), made famous by the movie The Man with the Golden Gun . You can also visit Koh Panyee, a unique floating village where you can experience local life and enjoy fresh seafood. Phang Nga Bay is perfect for kayaking through hidden caves and lagoons, offering a tranquil and scenic adventure. 2. Visit the Phi Phi Islands The Phi Phi Islands are a must-see on any yacht charter from Phuket. These world-famous islands are known for their stunning cliffs, azure waters, and vibrant marine life. Maya Bay, on Phi Phi Leh, became famous after its appearance in the movie The Beach and is one of the most photographed spots in Thailand. bay offers excellent snorkeling and swimming opportunities. For those looking to explore below the surface, the waters around the Phi Phi Islands are perfect for diving, with vibrant coral reefs teeming with tropical fish. 3. Discover Coral Island (Koh Hae) If you’re looking for a closer destination, head to Coral Island, also known as Koh Hae, just south of Phuket. This island is famed for its colorful coral reefs, making it an excellent spot for snorkeling. Long Beach and Banana Beach are both great for sunbathing or exploring the underwater world with a snorkel. The island’s shallow waters make it perfect for families or anyone looking for a relaxing day in paradise. 4. Sail to the Racha Islands For those seeking tranquility, the Racha Islands (Koh Racha Yai and Koh Racha Noi) offer an escape from the crowds of Phuket. These islands are known for their crystal-clear waters, which make them ideal for snorkeling and diving. The beaches are less developed than other tourist hotspots, giving visitors a peaceful and serene experience. Koh Racha Yai, in particular, features white sandy beaches and a relaxed atmosphere, making it a great place to unwind and soak in the natural beauty of Thailand. 5. Snorkel and Kayak Around Koh Yao Islands The Koh Yao Islands, located between Phuket and Krabi, offer a peaceful alternative to the more famous islands. Koh Yao Yai and Koh Yao Noi are less developed, making them perfect for those who want to experience authentic Thai island life. The islands are great for snorkeling, kayaking, and beach-hopping. The surrounding waters are calm, making for relaxed sailing conditions. You can also explore traditional fishing villages and learn more about the local culture. Dream Yacht’s Charter Options in Thailand Dream Yacht offers a variety of charter options in Thailand , catering to different sailing preferences. For experienced sailors, Bareboat Charters allow you to explore the Andaman Sea at your own pace. If you prefer a more guided experience, Crewed Charters come with a professional crew who will take care of navigation and meal preparation, allowing you to focus on relaxing. For those who don’t want to charter an entire yacht, our range of By the Cabin Charters in Thailand are a great option, where you can book a cabin on a shared yacht and still enjoy the services of a qualified local skipper and on board Hostess/Chef. item.title: How to Travel Around the BVIs by Yacht
item.description: (A Review by the Gypsy Nesters) In November our friends and professional baby boomer travel bloggers, the Gypsy Nesters , began an eight day jaunt across the British Virgin Islands and St. Martin aboard the sailing catamaran, Dream Canouan on our BVI Dream Premium cabin charter. The Gypsy Nesters sold their house after their last child left home and began an adventure that has taken them all around the world and resulted in an Amazon bestseller. Their mini cruise included stops and overnight anchorages at several out of the way places, such as Jost Van Dyke, Sandy Cay, The Baths on Virgin Gorda, Anegada, the caves at Norman Island and Grand Case, none of which are even remotely possible to reach on larger ships. They traveled from St. Martin to the BVIs and, the Gypsy Nesters say the people of the BVIs are resilient and have come a long way in re-building and welcoming back charterers. Foxy’s is back open with their drinks, food and music along with other local hot-spots that have reopened with vigor. The natural beauty has also made its return, just follow their BVI journey below with some breathtaking photo highlights . In regards to how they felt about traveling to the BVIs, where they once lived. The Gypsy Nesters said: “As soon as we stepped off the plane in St. Martin we felt at home. “The warm tropical breeze filled our senses and immediately took us back to when we lived on St. Croix in the US Virgin Islands. Having spent nearly a decade down here, we have learned a few things about the Caribbean. “One is that often the best places to visit are not the ones that are easily accessible to most tourists. If you come on a cruise ship you are likely to miss many of them as you hurry from one major port to the next.” See where their adventure took them and why travelling on a chartered boat is a more up close and personal way to experience the islands. Read more here . Not All to Discover in the BVI is by Sailing “The Islands of the British Virgin Islands are practically paradise with their vast white sand beaches stretching out under swaying palms and lush mountains rising above to the sky. However, that is only half of the picture. There is an equally amazing world of colors and scenery, along with an incredible collection of marine wildlife, to be discovered beneath the crystal blue water. We have always felt like it is akin to swimming in an aquarium.” The Gypsy Nesters’ under water experience can be seen in photos here . Leaving their Yacht The Gypsy Nesters’ last thoughts: We have to say that we now understand the desire to own your own secluded piece of paradise better than ever. Still, all in all we’d rather be seeing it from a boat. The only bad part of the trip was having to put shoes back on at the end. See the rest of the Gypsy Nesters journey here . … the best places to visit are not the ones that are easily accessible to most tourists.
